issues.legal_issue: A court that previously received a decree for execution may retain or regain authority to execute it when the court that passed the decree later authorizes execution, even if required transmission documents are not sent again.
material_facts: The court that passed the decree had transmitted it to another court for execution, and the transmitted decree and related documents remained on that court’s records.

The first execution application was dismissed for default, after which the executing court sent the decree court a document purporting to be a certificate of non-satisfaction, but did not return the decree documents.

The decree-holder later sought directions from the court that passed the decree, and that court, after notice to the judgment-debtors, authorized the executing court to sell the charged property in execution.
The order authorizing the sale was communicated to the executing court, which then proceeded with the sale.
issues.conclusion: The later order was in substance an order transmitting the decree for execution; the failure to resend the decree and a fresh certificate of non-satisfaction was an irregularity that did not deprive the executing court of jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 39 and 41 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and Order XXI, rule 6, the court that passed a decree may send it to another court for execution, and the Code does not prescribe a particular form for an order of transmission. An omission to send a copy of the decree or the prescribed certificate does not necessarily prevent execution where the decree and relevant documents are already with the executing court; such an omission may be a procedural irregularity rather than a defect in jurisdiction. The court relied on the terms and effect of the later order and did not identify a particular earlier case as authority for this conclusion.

rule.if: execution_proceeding and decree_previously_transmitted and later_execution_authorization_communicated and prior_decree_documents_retained

predicates.execution_proceeding: The matter concerns a court proceeding to enforce a decree.
predicates.decree_previously_transmitted: The court that passed the decree had previously sent it to another court for execution.
predicates.later_execution_authorization_communicat: The court that passed the decree later authorized execution by the other court, and that authorization was communicated to it.
predicates.prior_decree_documents_retained: The decree and related documents previously sent to the other court remained available on its records.

issues.definition: When a decree has previously been sent for execution, the decree court later authorizes execution, that authorization is communicated, and the decree documents remain with the executing court, the executing court has authority to proceed.

issues.legal_issue: A judgment-debtor may be barred by constructive res judicata from later challenging an executing court’s jurisdiction when the objection could and should have been raised in earlier execution proceedings but was omitted or abandoned.
material_facts: The judgment-debtor received notice of a second execution application but did not then object that the executing court lacked jurisdiction.

The judgment-debtor also received notice of the decree-holder’s application to the court that passed the decree for authority to sell the property, but did not object to the executing court proceeding.
The judgment-debtor challenged sales in several later applications and proceedings, but either omitted the jurisdiction objection or raised it without pressing it; the resulting orders became final.
The judgment-debtor raised the objection in a later application after the property had been sold and the execution proceedings had advanced.
issues.conclusion: The judgment-debtor was precluded from raising the jurisdiction objection at the later stage by constructive res judicata, notwithstanding that the objection concerned the executing court’s jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: The principle of constructive res judicata applies to execution proceedings even though section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, does not apply to them in terms. Under section 11, Explanation IV, and general principles of res judicata, a party is barred from raising later a matter that could and should have been raised earlier; an objection raised but not pursued may be treated as having been decided against that party. The jurisdictional character of the objection does not by itself prevent the rule from operating in these circumstances. The court relied on Annada Kumar Roy v. Sheik Madan, Mahadeo Prasad Bhagat v. Bhagwat Narain Singh, Ram Kirpal Shukul v. Mussamat Rup Kuari, Raja of Ramnad v. Velusami Tevar, and Sha Shivraj Gopalji v. Edappakath Ayissa Bi; it distinguished Ledgard v. Bull and other authorities, and overruled Raghubir Saran v. Hori Lal.

rule.if: execution_proceeding and party_had_opportunity_to_raise_objection and objection_could_have_been_raised_earlier and (objection_omitted or objection_abandoned) and earlier_proceedings_became_final

predicates.execution_proceeding: The matter concerns a court proceeding to enforce a decree.
predicates.party_had_opportunity_to_raise_objection: The party received notice or otherwise had an opportunity to raise the objection in the earlier proceedings.
predicates.objection_could_have_been_raised_earlier: The objection was available to the party at an earlier stage of the proceedings.
predicates.objection_omitted: The party did not raise the objection at an earlier stage when it could have done so.
predicates.objection_abandoned: The party raised the objection earlier but did not pursue it for decision.
predicates.earlier_proceedings_became_final: The earlier proceedings or orders concluded without the objection being determined in the party’s favour.

issues.definition: In execution proceedings, when a party had an earlier opportunity to raise an available objection, omitted or abandoned it, and the earlier proceedings became final, the party is barred from raising it later.
